adventure.title: Ferry to Algiers Point
adventure.description: The Canal Street ferry crosses the Mississippi in five minutes for pocket change — wander Algiers Point's gingerbread cottages, grab a drink at the corner bar, and ride back at golden hour.
adventure.bonus: Time the return crossing for sunset — the skyline from mid-river is the whole show.

adventure.title: Walk the Moonwalk Along the Mississippi at Dusk
adventure.description: The Moonwalk boardwalk just below Jackson Square puts you right at the river's edge as the tankers pass and the sky goes orange — it's free and it never gets old.
adventure.bonus: Sit on the river steps until the sun is fully down, then dip your hand in the Mississippi and let it dry on its own.

adventure.title: Mardi Gras Indian Super Sunday in the Seventh Ward
adventure.description: On the Sunday nearest St. Joseph's Day, the Mardi Gras Indians emerge in full hand-sewn suits of feathers and beads — it is the most visually overwhelming street spectacle in America.
adventure.bonus: Get close enough to see the bead stitching on a chief's suit and ask him how many hours it took — chiefs almost always tell you.

adventure.title: Give the WWII Museum the Full Day
adventure.description: The National WWII Museum is the best-reviewed museum in America for a reason — the immersive Road to Tokyo and Solomon Islands galleries alone deserve half a day, and the 4D film earns its hype.
adventure.bonus: Find a veteran's oral history station, listen to one full testimony without skipping, and write down one detail that sticks with you.

adventure.title: Sunrise at Crescent Park on the Riverfront
adventure.description: The best river view in the city is from the curved promenade in Crescent Park in the Bywater, where the Mississippi bends and cargo ships drift past at eye level.
adventure.bonus: Watch until at least one cargo ship passes, count its flags, and find out where it's registered before you leave.

adventure.title: Ghost Tour in the French Quarter with Haunted History Tours
adventure.description: Haunted History Tours has been leading lantern-lit walks past the Lalaurie Mansion and the Sultan's Palace since 1994 — their guides actually know the history.
adventure.bonus: Press your palm flat against the Lalaurie Mansion wall at 1140 Royal Street and hold it there for thirty seconds — report what you feel to the group.

adventure.title: Ride the St. Charles Streetcar to the End of the Line
adventure.description: The oldest continuously operating streetcar line in the world runs twelve miles through oak tunnels and uptown splendor for a dollar and a quarter.
adventure.bonus: Ride all the way to the Carrollton terminus, get off, buy a snowball from Hansen's Sno-Bliz, and ride back without consulting your phone once.

adventure.title: Gas-Lamp Stroll Through the Garden District
adventure.description: After dinner, the grand antebellum mansions on Prytania and Coliseum go quiet — gas-lamp glow, jasmine-heavy air, and live oak shadows all the way to Lafayette Cemetery's walls.
adventure.bonus: Find Anne Rice's former house at 1239 First Street, stand at the gate, and read aloud the first paragraph of Interview with the Vampire.

adventure.title: Second Line on Sunday with the Tremé Sidewalk Steppers
adventure.description: Every Sunday from fall through spring, a Social Aid and Pleasure Club parades through neighborhood streets and the whole city dances behind them — no ticket required.
adventure.bonus: Lock eyes with a brass band member and wave your handkerchief until they play a song just for you — then tip the band.

adventure.title: Swamp Tour at Honey Island Swamp
adventure.description: An hour east of the French Quarter, Honey Island is one of the least-altered river swamps in America — alligators surface close enough to make you flinch.
adventure.bonus: Ask your guide to cut the motor and hold your hand over the water for ten seconds while an alligator is visible.

adventure.title: Tour St. Louis Cemetery No. 1
adventure.description: The oldest above-ground cemetery in the country — Marie Laveau's tomb included — admits visitors only with a licensed guide these days, and the stories are worth every dollar of the ticket.
adventure.bonus: Find the tomb of Marie Laveau and leave an offering — a coin, a flower, anything — then make a wish out loud.

adventure.title: Night Kayak on Bayou St. John
adventure.description: Paddling through the dark cypress-lined bayou at night hits different — the city glows behind you and the water is dead quiet.
adventure.bonus: Cut your paddle, drift in silence for a full minute, and listen for the great horned owls that nest in City Park.

active.title: Sunset Pickup at The Fly
active.description: The riverside meadow behind Audubon Zoo is where the whole city comes to throw frisbees, kick soccer balls, and watch ships slide past at eye level — join whatever game finds you.
active.bonus: Get pulled into a game with strangers and stay until the ships turn their lights on.

active.title: Session at the New Orleans Boulder Lounge
active.description: The city's dedicated bouldering gym packs problems into an old St. Claude warehouse with a tight, welcoming crew — chalk up and flail until something clicks.
active.bonus: Finish one problem a full grade above your comfort zone — falling counts as research.

active.title: Sunrise Fishing Off the Seabrook Bridge
active.description: Local anglers have worked the tidal waters of Lake Pontchartrain from this bridge for generations — bring a rod, a cooler, and nothing pressing until noon.
active.bonus: Ask the first fisherman you see what they're using for bait and copy their exact setup — compare catches by 8am.

active.title: Kayak the Manchac Swamp at Sunset
active.description: Launch from the edge of Lake Pontchartrain into the cypress-draped silence of Manchac Swamp just as the light turns orange and the egrets come home to roost.
active.bonus: Paddle at least a half-mile past where you feel comfortable, cut your paddle out of the water, and just listen for two full minutes.

active.title: Climb the Monkey Hill at Audubon Zoo
active.description: Audubon Zoo has been a Uptown anchor since 1884 and Monkey Hill — the highest natural point in New Orleans — gives kids and adults alike a ridiculous thrill for a city technically below sea level.
active.bonus: Find the Louisiana swamp exhibit and identify every native species on the signage before you leave — no looking them up beforehand.

active.title: Tennis at the City Park Tennis Center
active.description: City Park's sprawling public tennis complex has been a neighborhood anchor for decades — book a court cheap and play in the shadow of ancient oaks.
active.bonus: Challenge a stranger on the next court to a single tiebreak set — loser buys a round at the nearest bar afterward.

active.title: Saturday Bike Ride with Confederacy of Cruisers
active.description: This long-running guided neighborhood bike tour moves through the city's most character-packed streets with a pace loose enough to actually stop and absorb things.
active.bonus: Ask your guide the one neighborhood fact they never get to tell tourists — and verify it independently afterward.

active.title: Run Audubon Park's 1.8-Mile Loop at Dawn
active.description: The shaded 1.8-mile perimeter path of Audubon Park loops past ancient oaks and a lagoon patrolled by egrets and night herons — one of the best urban runs in the South.
active.bonus: Run the loop twice without stopping, then cool down at the lagoon and stay long enough to spot at least three different bird species.

active.title: Wander Bywater on Foot at Golden Hour
active.description: The Bywater neighborhood's blocks of rainbow-painted Creole cottages and shotgun doubles look best when late afternoon light hits them — no agenda required.
active.bonus: Find a piece of public street art you've never seen photographed online and document it — extra points if the artist has signed it.

active.title: Canoe Rental Through City Park's Lagoons
active.description: Rent a boat at the Big Lake boathouse and thread City Park's interconnected lagoons under ancient live oaks and past heron rookeries — a disappearing act in the middle of the city.
active.bonus: Paddle to the most secluded stretch of lagoon you can find, cut the engine, and sit in silence for a full five minutes before heading back.

active.title: Bike the Lafitte Greenway Across Mid-City
active.description: This 2.6-mile converted rail corridor cuts through the heart of New Orleans connecting the Tremé to Bayou St. John with murals, community gardens, and zero car traffic.
active.bonus: Stop at every piece of street art along the trail and photograph only the one you'd actually hang in your home.

active.title: Run the Levee Trail from The Fly
active.description: The levee-top Mississippi River Trail heads upriver from the Audubon riverfront with unobstructed views of the bend, the barges, and zero tourists — the local runner's secret.
active.bonus: Run until you spot a pelican — Louisiana's state bird hunts this stretch of river — stop, photograph it, and don't move until it flies.

chill.title: Wander the Besthoff Sculpture Garden
chill.description: Eleven free acres of world-class sculpture — Rodin to Kusama — set among City Park's lagoons and 200-year-old oaks, with mirrored pavilions floating over the water.
chill.bonus: Find the sculpture that stops you cold and sit with it for five full minutes.

chill.title: Afternoon at the Backstreet Cultural Museum in Tremé
chill.description: This fiercely independent museum in the heart of Tremé holds the world's most important collection of Mardi Gras Indian suits, Social Aid and Pleasure Club regalia, and second line artifacts.
chill.bonus: Ask the curator or docent which tribe's suit took the most years to make — and find out what materials went into it.

chill.title: Spend a Morning at the Historic New Orleans Collection on Royal Street
chill.description: This research center and museum complex in the heart of the French Quarter holds the city's most extraordinary archive of maps, photographs, and manuscripts — and it's free.
chill.bonus: Ask a staff member to show you the oldest document in the current exhibition — then find the same street on a modern map and walk it afterward.

chill.title: Afternoon Porch Drink at Bouligny Tavern
chill.description: This low-key Uptown wine bar with serious cocktails and a tight snack menu is exactly the kind of neighborhood spot New Orleans does better than anywhere.
chill.bonus: Order whatever the bartender would drink on their night off — no second-guessing, whatever they say goes.

chill.title: Morning Coffee at Spitfire Coffee on St. Peter
chill.description: This tiny French Quarter espresso bar has no seating, no Wi-Fi, and no nonsense — just properly pulled shots and a front-row view of the Quarter waking up.
chill.bonus: Drink your espresso standing outside and say good morning to every local who walks past — count how many respond.

chill.title: Afternoon at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art
chill.description: The Ogden holds the most comprehensive collection of Southern art in the world and the building itself — a converted warehouse in the Warehouse District — is half the experience.
chill.bonus: Pick the one painting that unsettles you most and spend five full minutes with it before moving on.

chill.title: Evening on the Porch at Bacchanal Fine Wine
chill.description: This Bywater wine shop spills into a backyard where live jazz plays nightly and strangers share cheese boards and bottles under string lights until the night goes sideways.
chill.bonus: Let the shop staff choose your bottle completely blind — describe your night in one sentence and trust them.

chill.title: Sunday Morning at the French Market
chill.description: The oldest public market in the country still draws locals picking up local honey, Creole spices, and second-line umbrellas among the stalls that line the riverfront.
chill.bonus: Buy exactly one thing you have absolutely no use for and carry it proudly for the rest of the day.

chill.title: Drift Through the New Orleans Botanical Garden
chill.description: Tucked inside City Park, this WPA-built garden from the 1930s is one of the great undervisited spaces in the city — camellias, bromeliads, and ancient live oaks draped in Spanish moss.
chill.bonus: Find the oldest-looking oak in the garden, sit under it for ten minutes with your phone face-down, and do nothing.

chill.title: Afternoon at the New Orleans Museum of Art in City Park
chill.description: NOMA sits in the middle of 1,300 acres of live oaks and its permanent collection of glass art, photography, and Louisiana portraiture is genuinely world-class.
chill.bonus: Find one piece in the Newcomb pottery collection and sketch it in your phone notes — describe it like you're writing the wall card.

chill.title: Browse the French Quarter's Faulkner House Books
chill.description: William Faulkner wrote his first novel in this townhouse at 624 Pirate's Alley — now it's an impossibly curated bookshop that smells like old paper and takes your whole afternoon.
chill.bonus: Ask the bookseller to recommend the single best New Orleans novel they've ever read, buy it, and start the first chapter before you leave Pirate's Alley.

chill.title: Afternoon Read in Audubon Park Under the Oaks
chill.description: The ancient live oaks in Audubon Park have been arching over the lagoon since before the Civil War — bring a book and park yourself under one until the light goes gold.
chill.bonus: Find the largest oak you can, put your back against it, and stay there for at least one full hour without checking your phone.

social.title: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival at the Fairgrounds
social.description: Jazz Fest is the single greatest American music and food festival — seven stages, hundreds of Louisiana food booths, and a lineup that reads like a hall-of-fame ballot, every late April and early May.
social.bonus: Skip the headliner set intentionally — find the smallest stage on the grounds during that slot and go all in on whoever is playing.

social.title: Catch a Pelicans Game at Smoothie King Center
social.description: New Orleans goes loud for the Pelicans — the downtown arena sits right beside the Superdome, and the energy on a good night is an essential city experience most visitors skip entirely.
social.bonus: Sit in the cheapest seats in the building and make at least two genuine friends before halftime.

social.title: Jazz at Preservation Hall on St. Peter Street
social.description: The original 1961 hall holds fewer than a hundred people in standing room and presents New Orleans traditional jazz every single night with no amplification and no frills.
social.bonus: Pay the extra fee to request a song — then dedicate it out loud to a stranger in the room.

social.title: Attend Sunday Mass at St. Augustine Church in Tremé
social.description: Founded in 1841 by free people of color, St. Augustine is the oldest African American Catholic parish in the country and its gospel-infused Sunday liturgy is genuinely transcendent.
social.bonus: Stay after the service to speak with a parishioner and ask them what St. Augustine means to their family — really listen.

social.title: Live Zydeco at Rock 'n' Bowl on Carrollton
social.description: This only-in-New-Orleans institution layers a full bowling alley under a dancehall where live zydeco and Louisiana roots music shake the floors most nights of the week.
social.bonus: Bowl exactly one frame, then abandon your lane for the dancefloor — let a stranger teach you a zydeco step before the set ends.

social.title: Gallery Hop on Julia Street in the Warehouse District
social.description: New Orleans' densest corridor of serious contemporary art galleries turns into an open social scene every first Saturday of the month during Art Walk.
social.bonus: Walk into at least three galleries and ask a gallerist which piece in the room is the most underrated — then buy a postcard or small print from your favorite.

social.title: Neighborhood Cocktails at Twelve Mile Limit
social.description: This Mid-City neighborhood bar pours some of the most inventive, affordable cocktails in the city to a crowd that actually lives here.
social.bonus: Strike up a conversation with a stranger at the bar and get a local restaurant recommendation you've never heard of — then write it down and actually go.

social.title: Late Night at the Maple Leaf Bar for Rebirth Brass Band
social.description: Every Tuesday for over 30 years Rebirth Brass Band has packed this Riverbend bar to the point of structural concern — it is the loudest, sweatiest, most joyful room in New Orleans.
social.bonus: Get as close to the front as possible and dance without stopping for an entire song — no phones, no excuses.

social.title: Jazz Brunch at Commander's Palace
social.description: The weekend jazz brunch at this Garden District landmark has been the pinnacle of New Orleans dining since 1893 — white tablecloths, turtle soup, and a live trio working the dining room.
social.bonus: Order the full 25-cent martini flight, tip your server outrageously well, and tip-toe through the kitchen tour if they offer one.

social.title: Show Night at Tipitina's
social.description: The legendary Uptown hall that Professor Longhair built still runs local bills early in the week when the crowd is entirely New Orleans — stand under the Fess bust and let the room do the rest.
social.bonus: Learn the name of the headlining musician before you leave and find one of their albums to play on the way home.

social.title: Drinks at Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop Bar
social.description: Built before 1772 and allegedly used by the pirate Jean Lafitte, this candlelit brick cottage on Bourbon Street is the oldest bar structure in the United States and still feels like a hiding place.
social.bonus: Order a Purple Drank, find a seat in the darkest corner, and introduce yourself to the next person who sits near you — tell them the bar's history.

social.title: Late Night at Frenchmen Street with No Plan
social.description: Frenchmen Street in the Marigny is where New Orleans actually goes to hear live music — three blocks of bars spilling brass and jazz onto the sidewalk every single night.
social.bonus: Walk into whichever bar has the loudest music, tip the band twenty dollars, and stay for the next full set without leaving.

foodie.title: Tasting Menu at Compère Lapin
foodie.description: Chef Nina Compton fuses Caribbean and New Orleans Creole in a hotel kitchen that punches so far above its weight class it's won a James Beard Award to prove it.
foodie.bonus: Ask the sommelier to pair each course with a Louisiana-made wine or spirit only — no imports tonight.

foodie.title: Banh Mi at Dong Phuong, New Orleans East
foodie.description: The James Beard-honored bakery at the heart of the Versailles Vietnamese community bakes the bread half the city's banh mi ride on — go early, buy pastries for later, thank yourself.
foodie.bonus: Order in whichever dish you can't pronounce on the menu and eat the whole thing without googling what's in it.

foodie.title: Cocktails at Cure on Freret
foodie.description: Cure pioneered the serious cocktail movement in New Orleans and the bar's precise, spirit-forward drinks in a converted firehouse still set the standard a decade later.
foodie.bonus: Tell the bartender your mood in three words and let them build you something off-menu — no veto allowed.

foodie.title: Crawfish Boil at the Backyard of Middendorf's
foodie.description: This Manchac institution an hour from the city has been piling boiled seafood on picnic tables over a cypress swamp since 1934 — the thin-fried catfish alone is worth the drive.
foodie.bonus: Peel and eat an entire pound of crawfish using only one hand while holding a cold Barq's in the other.

foodie.title: Red Beans and Rice Monday at Liuzza's by the Track
foodie.description: Every Monday the city eats red beans and rice, and Liuzza's version near the Fairgrounds is the benchmark — slow-cooked, smoky, and poured over rice in a bowl the size of your ambitions.
foodie.bonus: Order a Abita draft with your beans and make a toast to the tradition with whoever's sitting next to you at the bar.

foodie.title: Raw Oysters at Casamento's
foodie.description: This tile-covered Uptown institution has been shucking Gulf oysters since 1919 and the ice-cold dozen at the bar is one of the purest eating experiences the city offers.
foodie.bonus: Eat a full dozen raw at the bar without adding any hot sauce — just lemon and let the Gulf do the talking.

foodie.title: Dinner at Arnaud's in the French Quarter
foodie.description: One of the grande dame Creole restaurants of New Orleans, Arnaud's has been serving shrimp remoulade and pompano under crystal chandeliers since 1918.
foodie.bonus: After dinner, slip upstairs into the free Mardi Gras museum and try on a vintage carnival costume if staff lets you.

foodie.title: Lunch Counter at Domilise's Po-Boy Shop
foodie.description: This Uptown shotgun shack has been slinging shrimp and roast beef po-boys since 1918 and every sandwich still tastes like someone's grandmother made it.
foodie.bonus: Order the half-and-half dressed and eat it at the counter without using a single napkin — good luck.

foodie.title: Lunch at Café Reconcile
foodie.description: This Central City institution trains young people for hospitality careers while serving some of the most honest Southern lunch plates in the city — the shrimp Creole funds a future.
foodie.bonus: Strike up a real conversation with your server about the program — ask them what dish they're most proud of making.

foodie.title: Dinner at Galatoire's on a Friday
foodie.description: Friday lunch and dinner at Galatoire's on Bourbon Street is a city institution since 1905 — regulars in seersucker suits hold court for four hours and the waiter knows everyone's name.
foodie.bonus: Order the Godchaux salad tableside, strike up a conversation with the table next to you, and find out how long they've been coming here.

foodie.title: Morning Beignets at Café Du Monde
foodie.description: Open since 1862 and covered in powdered sugar before 8 a.m. — Café Du Monde on the edge of Jackson Square is the oldest ritual in the city and it earns the hype.
foodie.bonus: Eat your beignets fast enough that you inhale the powdered sugar — you'll cough, the table will laugh, and you'll be doing it exactly right.

foodie.title: Lunch at Dooky Chase's Restaurant
foodie.description: Leah Chase's Tremé institution has been feeding civil rights leaders, presidents, and neighborhood regulars since 1941 — the fried chicken and red beans are not negotiable.
foodie.bonus: Order a dish you've never eaten before, ask your server who Leah Chase's most famous regular was, and repeat the answer to someone today.
